speechtext:
1.	Has the government received, from the labour congresses and/or from other organizations, representations asking that the National Housing Act be amended so as to forbid any refusal to sell or rent homes built under the provisions of the said act, where such refusal is based on grounds of race, colour or creed?
2.	Will consideration he given to the introduction of such an amendment to the National Housing Act?

Mr. Speaker, the answer to the first part of the question is yes, we have received one or two such representations. I am glad to say, however, that the cases of discrimination which have been brought to our attention have been very few.
Regarding the second part of the question, when the National Housing Act was being revised in late 1953 and early 1954 one organization did make representations. The government is firmly in accord with the principle of non-discrimination and we, therefore, had full and friendly discussions with this organization which was most co-operative and understanding. We concluded at that time, however, that nothing useful would be accomplished by amending the act.
We have subsequently again gone fully into the difficulties involved in any attempt to enforce non-discrimination, having in mind the nature of the transactions under the National Housing Act.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is removed some steps from the vendor-purchaser relationship and the landlord-tenant relationship in respect of houses financed under the act. A loan is obtained by a builder from an approved lender, and the lender receives an insurance policy from the corporation. There is no contract in respect of an insured loan between the corporation and the borrower. In other words, the transaction is between the lender and the borrower, not between Central Mortgage and the borrower.
When the house or project is completed the owner is free to deal with it in accordance with the provincial laws, subject only to the
first mortgage on it. Sales take place and apartments are rented without the corporation's prior knowledge of the transactions. Even the approved lender, who is one step closer to the vendor-purchaser, landlord-tenant relationships than the corporation, would I believe find itself in an ineffective position in trying to enforce a clause such as has been suggested.
Under the circumstances and inasmuch as the government endorses the principle of non-discrimination, we have not been able to convince ourselves that the answer to the problem is through an amendment to the National Housing Act.

1.	Has the Canadian government or any department received any requests for assistance in the construction of a traffic tunnel between the city of Toronto and Toronto island?
2.	If so, has any decision been made by the Canadian government, and what decision?
3.	Does the Canadian government recognize any obligation by agreement or otherwise to construct or share in the cost of constructing such a tunnel?

The records show that from time to time, almost since the beginning of the century, there has been correspondence in connection with a proposed traffic tunnel between the city of Toronto and Toronto island. In recent years, however, we have received no official representations.
On November 1, 1952, the then minister of public works wrote to the then mayor of Toronto, and I quote the last paragraph from his letter:
As representations have been made on numerous occasions, all informal, some of which favoured the

connecting of the island and the mainland, and others which opposed it most strongly, I do not feel that the dominion government should influence these two lines of thought by indicating their willingness to proceed with the construction of either a tunnel or a bridge. I think in fairness to ourselves, who, after all, entered into the agreement some 39 years ago, you should provide us with the guidance that represents the views of the city and thereby avoid our having to decide a problem on which there is divided opinion.
Apparently, the word "agreement" used in this context refers to an order in council, P.C. 1426, dated June 10, 1913. It was rescinded by order in council, P.C. 3926, dated December 23, 1935. In the meantime some of the work outlined in the order in council was completed at a cost considerably in excess of the total expenditure contemplated in the order in council.
Having in mind the federal government's attitude as expressed in the above-mentioned letter of my predecessor, as well as the fact that the only undertaking on record was made almost 43 years ago and has since been

rescinded, and that in discharging some of its terms considerably more money was spent by the federal government than was originally agreed, the Canadian government does not now recognize any obligation by agreement or otherwise to construct or share in the cost of constructing such a tunnel.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I moved the adjournment of this debate last night I was discussing the proposition that the government should take steps to ensure the maximum processing of raw materials at home before export. In this relation I was also discussing the problem of the development of our secondary industries, and the effect that such a proposition would have upon the expansion of our primary industries. I pointed out that in my opinion the only way the government could step in to ensure the maximum processing of raw materials at home would be to artificially encourage the further expansion of secondary industries. I further submitted that if the government were to move into this field and encourage the establishment of such industries in Canada, and if these industries came in under circumstances where their operations were uneconomic, then those industries would have every right to return to the government and ask for subsidies or protection. I pointed out that the inevitable result of such a policy would be the complete dislocation and unbalance of our economy. It would result in the necessity of protecting these industries and the primary result would be that the expansion of our primary industries, which are so dependent upon foreign markets, would be curtailed and particularly in the prairie provinces the expansion of primary industry within those provinces would also be curtailed.
In my concluding remarks, Mr. Speaker, I pointed out that since 1932 the average ad valorem rate of tariff on dutiable imports had been reduced by 40 per cent, from an average of 30 per cent to an average of 18-1 per cent.
I would point out to the house that the export of raw materials from Canada has from 1939 to 1954 increased by 288 per cent. On the other hand, our exports of manufactured and partially manufactured products have increased by 280 per cent, which indicates that the expansion of our secondary industries has kept pace with our export of raw materials. This is further indicated by the fact that the index of durable manufactures in 1939 was 107 -9; in 1954, it had risen to 297-9; and in 1955, it had further increased to 324-9. In this category the index had practically tripled. With respect to nondurable manufacturing, the index in 1939 was 108-2; in 1954, it was 222-4; and in 1955, 235-3, which was more than double the 1939 figure. The partially and fully manufactured exports had risen from $511 million to $1,846 million, while our exports of raw materials had risen from $273 million to $1,062 million. These figures indicate that our secondary

maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY OF GARRY 27

speechtext:
industries have kept pace with the expansion of our economy. They have established themselves in this country where conditions have warranted it, and our exports have not been out of line as compared with the expansion of the Canadian economy. On the whole, I think this refutes the statement that Canadians are fast becoming hewers of wood and drawers of water.
The figure of $1,062 million which I quoted as the total exports will, however, stand further examination. When we break down these figures we find that the exports of agricultural products and of animal products, which are normally exported in the raw state, are approximately 75 per cent of our raw material exports. The remaining raw material exports which are mainly made up of forest and mineral products are roughly 25 per cent of our total export, or $303,700,000 in value. When we take a look at the import figures of raw materials we find that in this category, a category other than agriculture or animal products, our imports totalled $473 million as compared with exports of $303 million, which makes us not a net exporter but a net importer of raw materials in this class to the value of $170 million.
Reference has been made in the budget debate, Mr. Speaker, to the tariff board, which I understand was set up by the Conservative party, and which has been made full use of by the present government. The policy of referring tariff requests to the tariff board should be continued and encouraged. We had a report on the textile industry last year. A report on the potato industry is in the hands of the minister at the present time, and further inquiries are to be made into iron and steel. The tariff board makes a complete study of the need of the particular industry for further tariff protection. It makes a complete study of the impact that the granting of such protection will have on the Canadian economy as a whole. When these findings are put into the hands of the government it is possible for the government to make a rational decision in so far as any tariff adjustments are concerned, and these decisions are then made on a reasonable basis and not merely for political or other reasons.
I should like to refer for a moment to the question of sales tax. In the 1954 budget, equipment sold to or imported by municipalities for their own use and not for resale at a price in excess of $1,000 per unit, specially designed for use directly for road-making, road-cleaning, or fire-fighting, but not to include automobiles or ordinary trucks, was exempted from sales tax. Municipal revenues are dependent on the taxation of real property. This base of taxation has remained practically
The Budget-Miss Aitken constant, particularly with rural municipalities. In order to meet rising costs municipalities have found it necessary to substantially increase their mill rates and have had to go to their respective provinces for additional funds. In practically all the provinces these funds have been made available but they are not sufficient to meet the increasing expenditures of our municipal corporations.
The net result is that our municipalities are having a difficult time in meeting increasing demands for road building, drainage and road maintenance. If he cannot do it in this budget I suggest to the Minister of Finance that in the next budget he remove from the sales tax provision repair and replacement parts for the machinery which was exempted from sales tax in 1954. Repair and replacement parts for these particular items of equipment are quite expensive and form a large part of municipal expenditure. Therefore I would request the minister to give this matter his consideration.

Mr,
Speaker, I wish to speak briefly on one phase of the budget because I feel that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has a tiger by the tail in introducing a 20 per cent tax on the advertising content in Canadian editions of United States magazines. It seems to me that when such taxes are put on we just do not know where they will stop because even now there are rumblings-I am sure the minister has heard them-from Canadian advertising agencies. They are looking askance at branches of United States agencies in Canada. Will the government step in and put on a 20 per cent tax on all advertising placed by United States agencies in Canada or will the government claim that such agencies cannot come into Canada on a competitive basis?
What about the writers who supply fiction for Canadian magazines? I am sure the Canadian fiction writers would be only too happy to see a 25 per cent tax put on all fiction written by Americans and placed in Canadian magazines. However, I do not believe Canadian editors would be very happy with a tax like that because almost 100 per cent of the fiction printed in Canadian magazines is written by United States authors. Therefore I feel that the Minister of Finance has a tiger by the tail.
Since I came into this house I have heard quoted many words uttered by wise men of the past, and the other day I came across a quotation which I think the Minister of Finance may have heard. Sir John Macdonald once said:
Those who cared to be protected wanted all the protection they could get. They were like the squaw who said of whiskey-that a little too much was just enough.

The Budget

Miss Aitken
The Minister of Finance intimated the other night that this is not primarily a tax. I believe it is simply a discriminatory and punitive measure against certain magazines. On March 22 the Toronto Telegram called it a vicious tax and went on to say:
A striking example of the government's misuse of its taxing power to invade the right of free publication in Canada.
This tax is supposed to help Canadian magazines, and it may or may not do that. The advertiser still has freedom of choice as to where he will place his advertising. It is supposed to help Canadian magazines but what about the Canadian reader, the consumer? Will it help him? No, it will not. The two magazines most affected by this tax are Reader's Digest and Time, and these magazines are not duplicated in Canada and I do not believe that they will be duplicated in the foreseeable future because they are [DOT]costly magazines to produce and they can exist only on international mass circulation.
The Reader's Digest has an annual payroll of $1,250,000 in Canada. Time has 33 bureaux in Canada costing with taxes $4 million a year. If these two magazines decide to stay in Canada despite the 20 per cent tax the cost to them based on their 1955 advertising will be approximately $664,000 in the case of Time and $620,000 in the case of the Reader's Digest.
Quite aside from these two United States magazines published in Canada there are about seven others which will also be affected, although to a much lesser degree. That is, nine United States magazines are to be discriminated against at a time when there are actually 100 consumer magazines coming in here from the United States and circulating in Canada. Those 100 consumer magazines have a combined circulation of 5,929,329. This does not include trade journals.
If the two magazines most affected by this 20 per cent tax decide to get out of Canada and not try to compete with Canadian magazines it will mean that the government is penalizing the consumers as well as the publishers of the magazines. We readers will be deprived of magazines that we cannot get here under any circumstances.

I am not comparing Harper's Bazaar or the Atlantic Monthly with the Reader's Digest and Time. I am speaking about a special kind of magazine. As I said, we will be deprived of certain types of magazines because there is no Canadian magazine
IMiss Aitken.1

like these magazines. They are informative and popular and are not duplicated in this country. Personally I resent government interference in connection with my reading matter.
Then we come to another phase of this tax which can be interpreted as censorship. I feel that this tax is dangerous for the government to impose because of that possible interpretation. We do not like any form of censorship here in Canada. I think we are unanimous on that in this house. At the moment the Minister of Finance is confining himself to the advertising content, but what is to stop him from interfering with the editorial content as well? Or is this a form of censorship already? If these magazines move out it will mean that this is a form of censorship.
We know, for instance, that there is no love lost between Time and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). We know that there is no love lost between Time and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). In that connection I found a report in the New York Times most interesting. This was a straight factual report, but in the middle I found what could be described only as a deadpan observation. This paragraph reads:
The new tax hits Time magazine and Reader's Digest hardest.
Time recently has been attacking Lester B. Pearson, Secretary of State for External Affairs, as an appeaser in the Far East, referring to him on one occasion as "Nehru in a homburg hat".
This is an innuendo to which we may not necessarily subscribe, but the fact remains that the Minister of Finance has laid himself and the government open to such accusations.
Then I find, in the next phase, that this is completely inconsistent with other actions of the cabinet. The Minister of Finance has expressed in a very paternal way his concern over the future of Canadian magazines, and that is his reason for this tax. On March 15 the Secretary of State for External Affairs was expressing paternal concern over another phase of our life. He was asked in this house if he had made any protests to the United States government over potential legislation in some states which would discriminate against or even put out of business some Canadian brewing companies that wanted to open branches of their industry in the United States. The minister said that he had conveyed our concern to the United States government, and I quote his words on that occasion:
That concern is based wholly on the principle involved and not merely on the situation of any particular industry.
The United States authorities, up to now, have agreed with that principle involved and

they shared the minister's concern. But it seems to me that the same principle of discrimination is involved in this 20 per cent tax introduced by the Minister of Finance, which was our concern last week, on the other side of the penny.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), on the other hand, has no compunction about ushering in United States capital to finance and control part of our national resources. The Minister of Finance stands guard over Canadian magazines. The Secretary of State for External Affairs stands guard over the rights of Canadian brewers. Yet the Minister of Trade and Commerce ignores any principle involved. He is quite prepared to give United States businessmen control of our trans-Canada pipe line. I find this all very inconsistent.
Then we come to the results of the tax. I cannot imagine where the minister got this brain-wave of a tax. It certainly was not from the Massey report and, if you can believe the Massey report, it was not from the periodicals, unless there has been a change since the Massey report, because in the Massey report there is this piece of information:
We were impressed by the fact that Canadian periodicals neither desired nor requested any protective measures apart from an adjustment of tariff rates on paper imported from the United States for publishing purposes.
That is why I say I feel that the Minister of Finance has got the tiger by the tail. This is a punitive and discriminatory measure against nine magazines, but it does not stop there. This 20 per cent tax can penalize the consumer or reader who wants to read those magazines and read the Canadian news in those magazines. It can penalize the Canadian advertising agencies who want to place advertising in those magazines. It can penalize the research bureaux which are used extensively by these magazines. It can penalize the newsstand operators who sell these magazines. Finally, it can penalize the Canadian postal department.
Ministers of the crown are not very receptive to suggestions from this side of the house, but I have a suggestion to make. As I mentioned before, there are 100 consumer magazines that come over here from the United States and they are competing with Canadian magazines. Nine of these are published, distributed and mailed here in Canada, and Canadian postage is used. Ninety-one are published and mailed from the United States, with United States postage used. If we must give some protection to our Canadian magazines, why not put a postal tax on these publications that come into Canada? Then, if Canadians want to buy the magazines and
The Budget-Mr. Legate absorb the postal tax, they can do so to the benefit of our treasury. If they feel the cost is more than the magazine is worth, then they have the freedom of choice to take it or leave it. But to put an unfair and punitive tax on just a few of the United States magazines and ignore the others is, to me, an unprecedented and an un-Canadian act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes at my disposal, I shall emphasize some of the sound decisions that are found in the budget brought down last week by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris). The first that comes to my mind-no doubt because the opposition has been bitterly attacking it these last few days-is the government proposal to introduce a 20 per cent tax on advertising in Canadian editions of foreign publications.
What is the situation at this time? There are in this country three types of publications: Canadian publications put out by Canadians, for Canadians and for the benefit of Canadians; then foreign publications which come to us from great cities such as New York, London or Washington, which enter this country without difficulty and freely circulate here and finally a third and weakest type, that is Canadian editions of foreign magazines.
There is a tremendous difference between these various types of magazines. The proposed tax will be levied on the third type, that is on the Canadian editions of foreign publications. This 20 per cent tax will apply to the advertising content of those Canadian editions.
Most of those Canadian editions are, properly speaking, the original magazine from which a few pages have been taken out to be replaced by other pages containing material relating to Canada. They also contain advertisements from Canadian companies, generally obtained from Canadian advertising agencies, which means that those magazines, published for the most part in the United States and sold in Canada, are in a much better position than Canadian magazines.
In Canada, where the market is restricted by a population much smaller than that of the United States, we have modest magazines far less sumptuously garbed than certain foreign magazines, precisely because their circulation, equally modest, does not allow it. On

The Budget-Mr. Legate the other hand, in the United States, where the population is ten times that of Canada, huge circulations enable publishers to put out substantial magazines of a truly high artistic level. So the circulation of these American magazines being so much larger than the circulation of similar magazines in Canada, their advertising rates are bound to be lower than those of Canadian magazines. Consequently, Canadian editions published by Canadians for the benefit of Canadians cannot compete with American magazines that publish a Canadian edition.
I took it that the intention of this government was merely to balance the costs of production of these two types of magazines, so that the publisher would not have to cut down his budget which, to my mind, would be a very serious mistake. I must say right now that this decision was a very sound one and that it would have been highly regrettable to delay its application.
This decision will also have another effect when Canadian firms prepare their advertising budgets. Advertising in Canadian editions of foreign magazines means so much money lost to Canadian media. This I shall attempt to explain.
Let us suppose that a Canadian edition of a foreign magazine carries from $5,000 to $25,000 worth of advertising by Canadian firms. It is so much advertising denied Canadian publishers who cannot compete with the American publisher, whose production costs are lower because of very large circulation.
As a result of that 20 per cent tax-which, to my mind, is somewhat low, and which I would rather see a bit higher, because I believe it does not equal the production costs differential of United States and Canadian magazines-as a result of that 20 per cent tax on advertising in Canadian editions of foreign magazines, production costs will be better balanced, and so Canadian publishers will be in a better position to compete with those foreign magazines, most of which are but slightly modified editions of the original magazine published in the United States.
Approximately 250 magazines, called trade publications, are published in Canada, about half of them, or maybe less, printed in Ontario. Had the federal government delayed taking the steps announced in the budget speech, before long, and sooner than we think, we would have had to face a competition that would have threatened the existence and survival of numerous Canadian

publications. Let me give you an example. Practically all branches of commerce or industry have their own magazine. Jewelers have theirs, and so have contractors, hotel operators, etc. Let us, for instance, take the Canadian hotel operators' magazine.
It is an unpretentious, very well made and interesting magazine, but owing to the fact that we have a limited number of hotels in Canada its circulation is limited in this country. On the other hand, in the United States, with their much larger population, there are trade magazines for inn-keepers and hotelkeepers, and these magazines have a much larger circulation, which means that they are bigger and much more attractively printed. If the publisher of a trade magazine for American hotel-keepers decides to publish a Canadian edition, he will leave out a few pages of his national edition and replace them with some pages on Canada. And these pages will be accompanied by advertising of interest to Canadians, advertising of products or goods which are bought by hotel-keepers. Here you have two trade magazines. One is published by Canadians for Canadians, and it is small. The other, published in the United States for Americans, is much larger because, from its very beginning, it has enjoyed a large circulation in the United States, which means that it has been able to publish more articles in its original edition.
Of the two, the hotel keeper or operator will surely prefer the bulkier, more attractive one, with more reading matter, in short, the more complete one. The circulation of that foreign publication will inevitably rise in Canada at the expense of Canadian magazines for hotel men, builders or restaurant owners, in such a way that Canadian magazines will necessarily reduce their volume and, after "X" months,-I will not say "X" years,-will have to cut down further, or fold up, while the American magazine will establish itself in this country and will build up a circulation likely to compete unfairly with Canadian publications.
Another instance can be given to prove the soundness of this tax. We know that Life magazine publishes editions in many countries, France, England, Spain, Italy and that these editions are replicas of the American edition, published by the owners, in New York. Should the editors of Life decide tomorrow to publish a Canadian edition they will merely replace a few pages on their American national edition with a few pages

and photographs on Canada, and will then add pages of advertisements sought from Canadians through advertising agencies. This would be a Canadian edition of Life. But what would happen then? In each Canadian edition of Life magazine, if ever it comes out, we shall find 5, 10, 15, 20 or even 25 thousand dollars worth of ads that might otherwise have gone to the four advertising media in Canada.
My hon. friend from Calgary South (Mr. Nickle) said the other day that there is nothing to prove that this money would go to Canadian publishers. Nothing proves it, no, but we may rest assured that the budget not spent in foreign publications will be allocated to other advertising media in this country, such as magazines, newspapers, radio and television, or even bill boards. We are therefore assured that the advertising budget earmarked for Canada will be spent in Canadian magazines, published by and for Canadians.
It has been implied that by this measure we were seeking to bar the entry of foreign magazines into this country. This is quite untrue. Now or at any future time, any foreign magazine, of whatever origin, provided it passes the censor, will enjoy the privilege of entry into this country and of free circulation, unhampered by supplementary taxes, or higher postage rates.
Several members opposite have claimed that this legislation would deprive Canadians of magazines published outside this country, which is quite untrue. The purpose of the budget speech must be well understood in order to realize that the government does not propose to restrict nor embarrass in any way the circulation or the importation of foreign magazines into Canada. The only kind of magazines affected are the Canadian editions of foreign publications, whether they be published in the United States, in France or in London. Their number is now quite limited; but I think it could be said without exaggeration that certain signs justify the belief that their number will increase in the near future and that it would soon have constituted a serious threat to Canadian publishers. Had not the government decided to impose a tax on the commercial section of those Canadian editions, and it seems to me that the action of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) has been quite wise, this industry would have been seriously threatened in this country. I had already given some thought to this prob-
The Budget-Mr. Legate lem and 1 had been wondering what means could be found to force foreign editors to compete on equal ground with Canadian publishers. I think we have struck upon a happy formula, a genuine discovery, in taxing the Canadian advertising content of Canadian editions of foreign magazines.
I was astounded to hear the opposition criticize this measure. Why? Because, since the beginning of this session, the opposition has gone all out against United States investments in Canada, and hon. members will remember the protests raised by the opposition at the time the bill on the trans-Canada pipe line was introduced in this house. We were then told that control of the market was about to be taken over by the United States and that U.S. capital was encroaching upon our economy. Again a few days ago, the opposition criticized a bill concerning the extension of the Ungava railway. They claimed this was another privilege granted to the U.S., for the mere purpose of allowing them to take a firmer grasp on our country. And now, when the government is introducing a measure designed to protect the Canadian people, and to prevent Americans from taking too firm a hold on the magazine industry in this country, or even acquiring control of that industry, we see the opposition rise as one man in disapproval.
I hope that, despite those protests, the government will carry out its intentions, wishes and plans so that, at the beginning of January, as already announced, this measure will go into effect, because I believe that a remedy to the present condition has been long overdue, and so that a larger measure of protection be granted to our magazine publishers who, until now, have been alarmed by the encroachment of Canadian editions of foreign publications in this country, an encroachment which had tended to increase and which would surely have materialized, according to the information I can get.
I should not like to labour the point. I have tried to be as plain as possible about it. In my opinion, the situation is crystal clear; the government's intention is praiseworthy and should be supported because we will be the first to benefit from it.
If there is one field of which we should keep control it is that of culture, of thought. We must keep the privilege of editing and managing our own publications. It is a field in which we cannot let American or European people, or people from other countries, get control.

The Budget-Mr. Legare
If we want our press to remain free, the Canadian publishing industry should be able to live and live well. We have no objection to letting foreign publications enter Canada. Personally, I would oppose any proposal of the government aimed at preventing it. Far from it, I know that it is not the government's intention to take steps in that direction; the government's intention is solely, as I stated at the beginning, to try and balance the cost of production of those two types of magazines: the Canadian magazines controlled, managed and published for the benefit of Canadians, on the one hand, and on the other, Canadian editions of foreign magazines, published by Americans for the benefit of Americans.
Another decision of the government which pleased me greatly concerns the "Caisses populaires" and credit unions.
Through the budget speech we learned that the government intended to call a meeting in Ottawa of the administrators of our credit unions in order to discuss the possibility of placing them on an equal footing with chartered banks as far as loans guaranteed by the government are concerned. I remember that last year when a bill to provide help for fishermen was before the house, several hon. members asked that credit unions-caisses populaires-be placed on an equal footing with chartered banks. In fact, when the bill came back to the house from the committee, we found to our satisfaction that credit unions had been placed on a par with the chartered banks.
I believe-if I rely on what I heard from the budget speech-that the government intends to put credit unions on the same basis as the chartered banks. To my mind, it is a sound idea; it is even a recognition of the work done by credit unions-especially those in the province of Quebec, which I know better than those of other provinces-which have shown that they deserve the same treatment' as other more influential financial institutions in this country.
Credit unions perhaps deserve such treatment in recognition of their contribution in the field of house building. They have been leaders and pioneers in that field in Canada; they have made it possible for hundreds and even thousands of Canadians to own their own house. Today the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation follows the same policy and I believe that both institutions should carry on and extend their activities in that field.

I admire credit unions which, in some cases, attach a particular importance to the moral guarantee offered by the borrower, while the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation considers mainly his income or his salary, making sure at the same time that he has a permanent or steady position while the credit union, without neglecting such points, takes a much greater account of the moral guarantee.
The same can be said for the type of construction. A credit union will give more consideration to the wish of a borrower to build a house of a given type which is to his liking or which fits in a particular district while the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will consider mainly whether the plan complies with the law and will stick to the standards set by the housing legislation.
Two other measures announced by the federal government the day before yesterday have also provided a great deal of satisfaction to the Canadian people, and more particularly to two classes.
The first was announced in this house by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) who told us that the unemployment insurance commission had decided to extend unemployment insurance benefits to bush workers even though in the past those workers might have refused employment in districts other than their own. This decision which came after a rather large number of meetings between the Department of Labour and the officials of the unemployment insurance commission has made it possible to correct an unfortunate state of affairs. In my own constituency, there were approximately one hundred lumbermen who had been deprived of these benefits because they had refused to take jobs in the Abitibi district, where conditions did not seem to be as favourable as in their own area. These hundred-odd lumbermen, on returning from the north shore-since most of our south shore lumbermen spend the winter on the north shore- were disappointed to learn that they were to be denied these benefits. I should think that our lumbermen, generally speaking, should be treated with a little more consideration. I am particularly sympathetic to the condition of this class of workers who, in this season of the year, leave their wives and children behind to go into the bush where they have to work hard, with axe or power saw, from sunup to sundown.
I suggest that if there is one group of people who deserve the benefits to which

they have contributed while on the job, it is those people. Unfortunately, there are instances where our bush workers are temporarily deprived of those benefits. Sometimes, the benefits are suspended for 5 or 6 weeks.
I have here a request made by a bush worker who, while in camp, learned that his house had burned down. He dropped everything, and rushed home to help his family and then, when he claimed unemployment benefits, he was told that an employee cannot draw benefits under the act when he leaves his job for reasons such as these.
It is the same thing with bush workers who are called back home on account of death in the family. These too are denied benefits for a period of some weeks. I believe that the arbitration board should be authorized to give all sympathy to such cases or given some latitude to judge on their merits, in certain cases, the reasons given for quitting the job.
The other measure I want to discuss is the decision of the government to continue for two years the floor price for butter. That decision was conveyed to us last Thursday by the Minister .of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). At the beginning of his statement the minister said that he would give the members an interesting message to take home with them for the Easter recess. Well, if the minister gave us that piece of news so that we would convey it to our electors, I have to tell him that the news reached our counties quite some time ago, for no sooner had it been broadcast on the radio than it was being repeated everywhere. I would say that no more interesting piece of news has been announced to our farmers since the beginning of this session.
Those who are in the dairy industry have been wondering for the past few months if the price of butter would remain stable or if it would come down to 55, 52, or 50 cents a pound because of the fact that this winter's surplus was slightly larger. This decision is to be commended and shows that the government was well acquainted with the farmer's position; indeed, the Minister of Agriculture and the members of the cabinet have immediately decided to extend for two more years the act relating to the support price of butter. As a result of this extension, I can imagine a sigh of relief from our farmers back home who find in the dairy industry a modest income to compensate for the losses they of necessity incur in other branches of their activities.
The Budget-Mr. Legare
It is a piece of news that rejoices the farmers and proves that this government is paying much more attention than might be realized to all the problems besetting the farmers.
In concluding, I would like to stress a very unhappy situation that exists in one of the Lower St. Lawrence districts, namely the present situation in the counties of Matane, Matapedia, and part of the county of Rimouski where drought caused damages valued at $5 million by the Catholic farmers' union. The farmers in these three Lower St. Lawrence counties suffered losses amounting to $5 million on account of last summer's drought, while they had lost hundreds of thousands of dollars on account of heavy rains the year before.
I am receiving petitions and requests from all over my constituency, from county and municipal councils, as well as from a great many farmers who are seeking federal support, because, they say, we will not be able to seed this coming spring, as the losses suffered last fall were too heavy. I sent the requests to the Minister of Agriculture, but he replied that he could do nothing unless requested to do so by the province of Quebec; it was the only reply he could give under the circumstances, as this is a matter of jurisdiction. It is recognized that no help can be given directly in the province of Quebec, either to an individual or a municipality unless a request to that effect is made by the provincial government. In recent days, the provincial government has decided to take the necessary steps, but by itself, and to spend between two and three hundred thousand dollars in the counties concerned. It will provide grants to some municipalities, asking them to distribute the money in the surrounding district to compensate farmers in drought areas for the cost of seed grain. The provincial government's grant might represent, let us say, half the cost of seeding in the counties concerned. I am confident that had the provincial government submitted a request to the federal government, the latter would have contributed a large amount, so that instead of receiving only partial compensation for the cost of their seed grain, our farmers would perhaps have been compensated for the whole amount. Had a committee been established to look into this matter, no doubt the central government would have investigated the possibility of compensating our farmers for the heavy losses they have sustained recently. Although a loss of $5 million in that area might not be a national calamity, it does

The Budget-Mr. Bryson affect the national economy, because that $5 million loss tor farmers of three constituencies will paralyse their operations, preventing them from buying farm machinery and improving their land as they would have liked to. Moreover, they will have trouble paying back their farm loan, at least those of them who had to mortgage their property.
In conclusion, I must say that I regret such a situation; I wish the federal government had been in a position to help alleviate the recent difficulties of farmers in that part of the Lower St. Lawrence. I hope that it is not too late and that the government of the province of Quebec will put its pride aside-if its decision was indeed inspired by pride-and will request the assistance of the central government for the benefit of those people whose difficulties I appreciate and to whom I extend my most sincere sympathy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of his remarks on Monday last my deskmate, the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron), pointed out to the house that he found to his amazement little or no reference of any kind whatsoever to the defence expenditures in the budget address. He concluded that among other things apparently the government expects the people of Canada to accept those expenditures as a matter of course, and it is quite unnecessary to explain these expenditures in spite of the fact that they do constitute well over half of government spending. I was rather amazed to find that in so far as agriculture is concerned little or no reference was made in the budget to that subject, either. It was rather astonishing to realize that the Minister of Finance found it necessary to use more than 12,000 words to set out Canada's economic position and to devote only two very short sentences to Canada's most important industry. Those two sentences are to be found at the bottom of page 2325 of Hansard, and I should like to quote them:
For example, wheat farmers had a much better than average crop, but during the first part of the crop year were unable to deliver as much as all of us would like to have seen. However, this has changed materially since the session began, and sales have greatly increased.
My first thought was that the minister had run out of paper. He would have given the house a more realistic picture of the agricultural position had he, following the word
fMr. Legare.l
"began", added: "and still the farmer's position is steadily deteriorating". I think that would have been a much more realistic statement. Therefore, the only conclusion I can come to is that this rather grave deliberate omission is further evidence that this government has relegated agriculture to the role of unimportance in this country.
The minister then went on to make some rather broad and general statements regarding the economic condition in this country. He said: "We have had a buoyant and successful year". Later on he said: "Our economy has advanced rapidly and continuously through 1955". It is because of those allembracing statements that I was prompted this afternoon to rise and take part in this debate. I feel that such broad and sweeping statements must not go unchallenged in view of the fact that we have in this country a very depressed section of our economy.
My concern for agriculture is basically justice for our farm families. I think it is undeniable-and it is something for which this government stands condemned and they must accept responsibility for it-that in the midst of this widespread prosperity in every other industry, to which the minister and his colleagues like to point with such pride, we have farm families and agriculture in general suffering from the heavy hand of poverty. I think it is clear that the government has failed to provide economic justice for that very large section of the Canadian people.
We talk about the great future of this country. I am sure that if we are to be a great nation this government must accept responsibility to see to it that all the citizens of this country are assured economic opportunities. Surely, it is the moral responsibility of any government to see that all of the people are guaranteed not only social and political justice but economic justice as well.
Every time agriculture is discussed in this house we have had it pointed out over and over again that that does not apply in so far as agriculture is concerned. When the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) rises in his place in this house, as he does on every occasion, and attempts to set out the farmer's position and the position of agriculture and quotes and persists in quoting gross farm income, he is doing an injustice; he is not only unfair to the farmer but he is casting doubt in the minds of great sections of people in other parts of Canada as to the

justification of the farmer in saying that he is not getting his fair share of the national income. This is a deliberate attempt to mislead and misrepresent the true position. I do not know who those economists are who bring those gross figures to the attention of the minister on every occasion, but I am convinced of this. If those economists had attended the school of hard economic facts that the farmers in Canada have attended they would have flunked out because after all it is the farm net income that is the important thing. It is the net farm income that pays the farmer's bills, and nothing else.
According to the latest dominion bureau of statistics' figures we have received, since 1945 there has been a steady decline in agricultural income in this country. Net income has dropped from a high of $2,154,527,000 in 1951 to $1,125,641,000 in 1954, a drop of 48-22 per cent throughout Canada. In that same period capitalization of Canadian firms rose from $5,671 million to $9,718 million, almost double. The prairie provinces suffered even worse, Mr. Speaker. In 1951, the net farm income of the prairie provinces amounted to $1,127,300,000. In 1954, the net farm income had fallen to $376 million, including inventory, a drop of 66-44 per cent. These are the cold, hard economic facts. That is the sorry record of agriculture in this country. Yet, on the other side of the ledger what do we find? We find that 25 companies in this country dealing directly with farmers had their average profits go up 402 per cent since 1946.
How does the government propose to solve the dilemma that agriculture finds itself in today? Well, apparently the best the government can do is to stand around like a stunned ox and hope that something turns up. The best they can do is to suggest that nothing short of an agricultural disaster is going to solve the problem. In the meantime the agricultural experts in the department continue to conjure up silly phrases. Seasonal fluctuations, they call them; temporary periods of adjustment. They say that slight difficulties are being encountered, that there is some buoyancy, and a good many other equally foolish phrases. The farmers are not impressed with that kind of diagnosis. They see in a 50 per cent cutback in their income, not something which is temporary, they see it as something which constitutes a major disaster.
I should like to ask members of the government who come from rural areas in
The Budget-Mr. Bryson Canada: Have you had any success in trying to convince the farmers in your area that their loss of purchasing power is not real? Have you had any success in trying to convince the farmers in your area that a 50 per cent drop in their purchasing power is just statistical? I believe it is time that Canadian agriculture had a bill of rights, and I suggest that that bill of rights should be premised on the principle that the family farm should be assured a parity income. I would be the first one to suggest that under certain circumstances it might be necessary to make subsidy payments, that under certain circumstances some support would have to be forthcoming to guarantee a parity income to the family farm. I believe that we must reestablish in many sections of Canada the family farm because it is the best possible type of land tenure we can have, because it will give assurance that we are going to maintain in this country the kind of community which we need, and with the continuance of that community life guarantee the maintenance of local government which in my opinion is the most important level of government.
The tendency in many parts of Canada is toward the corporation farm in the name of efficiency. As I have said in this house on other occasions, I am firmly convinced that we could not make a case in support of the family farm in the name of efficiency, but I believe there is something more involved than mere efficiency. We should learn from the lessons of history, because it is a fact that political freedom tends to disappear in any country that fosters a system of land tenure that builds up the corporation type of farm. Whether the land is under the control of individuals practising private enterprise or under the control of the state, as it is in the Soviet union, is of little consequence as both systems tend to rob the people of their political freedom.

One of the first things that General Mac Arthur did in Japan was to break up the large land holdings where the people were considered only as a part of the capital investment. So I say we should foster and develop the family farm as the best type of land tenure in order to maintain the political freedom and democracy which stems from local government.
I make my case for parity income on that basis. We are criticized when we talk about parity income or parity prices on the basis that it is going to cost the country something to maintain and support it. It seems to be perfectly all right for the taxpayers of this country to subsidize the Canadian Pacific, to subsidize the mining and oil industries, to subsidize by way of tariff the manufacturing industry of this country. We are told that that is wonderful, that is commendable, that is delightful, that is free enterprise; but when we ask that a subsidy be made available to agriculture we are told that is an entirely different matter, that is terrible, that is deplorable, that is impossible, that is socialism, that would be an attempt to corrupt and undermine the farmers' very moral fibre and would bankrupt the country.
As I listened to the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Thatcher) suggest that if all the legislation which had been sponsored and supported so far by the C.C.F. were carried out it would cost the people of Canada billions of dollars, I could not help but think how absolutely ridiculous such a statement was. We are worried about surpluses in this country because of overproduction. I agree that surpluses do come from overproduction, but surpluses occur whenever production exceeds the demand. In ail cases demand does not reflect need. I think it is important to remember that. Demand is restricted by the ability of people to buy, by their purchasing power. Until the domestic needs of this country are met, the genuine human needs, we would be well advised to refer to it as underconsumption rather than overproduction. When purchasing power falls to low levels and manufacturers find that their

consumer goods are starting to pile up, they overcome that situation quite easily by turning off their electricity and laying off workers. The result of course is that they do not have overproduction, that they do not have surpluses, but what is more important is that they do create a surplus of idle workers which is something infinitely worse in my opinion than overproduction.

There is no place in modern scientific agriculture for the argument that farmers do not necessarily have to rely on economics in order to carry on, that the farmer has some sentimental attachment, some sentimental affinity for the soil and for that reason will maintain his position regardless.
One of my constituents wrote to me and said, "I have a two-point program which I think would be very effective for agriculture in this country. I am sure, too, that the Minister of Agriculture would like to quit his cabinet post and retire to his farm at Melville, Saskatchewan.

After the department had supposedly carefully scrutinized this flock of sheep for two years and had given it a clean bill of health, the owner was allowed to show his sheep at the royal winter fair. The breeding stock were sold all over the country. Now they have destroyed the rest of the flock and are going to pay the owner some $90,000.
What about the people who bought stock from this flock that was sold at the royal winter fair? Are they to be left holding the bag? Why are not those sheep all called in and their owners treated in the same way this man in Alberta has been treated? There is an old saying, "It smells fishy". Well, this smells woolly to me. I am wondering whether it is more of a political debt than anything else. On top of that, the export market the sheep breeders of Canada have enjoyed for many years is endangered. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure we are all glad to see both the Prime Minister and the Leader
The Budget-Mr. Philpott of the Opposition back in their seats this afternoon. We are all particularly glad to see the Prime Minister back after another step in the policy he has been following of bringing about better relations among the nations of the world, especially among English speaking people. I sometimes ask myself how this government will go down in history, and I think among other things it will be classed as a great peacemaker government. While this government is naturally open to criticism on many scores I think in some things its record is beyond criticism, and at the top of that list would stand its record in making better relations among the nations of the world as well as right here in Canada.
When I heard the Minister of Finance present his fine, stable budget the other night, I could not help recalling the budget that we heard two years ago presented by his predecessor, Hon. Douglas Abbott. I think hon. members will remember that at that time the relations between this government and one of the provincial governments in Canada, that is the relations between the government of Canada and the government of the province of Quebec, were none too good. I think it is a great tribute to the peacemaking abilities of the present Prime Minister of Canada that that situation, which loomed so dark at that time, has now been completely resolved and harmony reigns.
While there are not many members from British Columbia left in the house, I see one or two, my good friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Barnett) and one or two others. Regardless of what political party we belong to, we shall all be glad that the relations between the government of British Columbia and the government of the Dominion of Canada-by the way, for the benefit of the last speaker, I am one of those who like the word "dominion" and I am proud of it-are now better than they have been since this strange government that we now have in British Columbia came into power a few years ago.
We will recall that at the second last meeting of the provincial premiers with the Prime Minister of Canada, if we can trust the newspaper accounts, the premier of British Columbia went home in a huff and would not even stay for the Prime Minister's tea party or dinner party, or whatever form the hospitality was taking. You recall that at the last meeting of the Prime Minister of Canada with the premiers of the provinces, the premier of British Columbia went home saying that all was sweetness and light and lauding the co-operation of this government to the skies.
I for one want to make it very clear that I hope that at the forthcoming meeting between

The Budget-Mr. Philpott the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources and the premier of British Columbia, we go a long way toward reaching solid agreement on the development of the water power of the upper Columbia river. I believe there is no undeveloped natural resource in all Canada that offers so much in the way of prosperity for all Canada as does the development of that great national water power resource. If we do work out the proper kind of co-operation between the Dominion of Canada and the province of British Columbia in regard to the development of the waters of the upper Columbia, we shall not need to fear further encroachment of United States private capital in this Dominion of Canada.
Turning to the actual amendment, I must say that I am shocked and astonished at the strange and contradictory attitude taken by Her Majesty's official opposition, that is, the official Conservative party. Here we have the hon. member for Greenwood moving an amendment reading in part as follows:
"this house regrets that the budget is empty, negative and partisan: that the government shows no concern over either the serious problems of distressed groups and areas or the growing economic domination of Canada by United States interests . . ."
I listened with great care to the long two-instalment speech of the official financial critic of the Conservative party and I reread it very carefully in Hansard. I cannot find one single word uttered by the official critic of the Conservative party in support of one of the finest moves that has been made by any Canadian government in recent years to end the threat of United States domination in one of the most vital sections of our whole national life in Canada; that is, by the common sense imposition of a fair and sane tax on what I would call the United States by-product magazines, the United States magazines that publish by-product editions in Canada. Perhaps I should say I do not know whether we should even use that word "publish" in connection with by-product editions in Canada. As a matter of fact one magazine, Time, is not even printed in Canada. It is printed in Chicago, as we all know.
However, my hon. friends in Her Majesty's official Conservative opposition held up their hands in holy horror at United States economic domination. Then we had speaker after speaker, beginning with the hon. member for Calgary South, then that long, and at least loud, speech by the hon. member for Eglinton, then the gracious lady member for York-Humber. After the strange silence on the part of Her Majesty's official financial critic, who did not even mention the matter, the
[Mr. Philpott.l
lesser lights in the Conservative party rose one after another and opposed this tax on United States magazines.
Surely the Conservative opposition will never be accused of having little minds. Who was the poet who said, "A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds"? We have them protesting strongly against United States economic domination of Canada and then, almost in the very next breath, they are protesting because the government has taken a step to guard against spiritual and mental domination of the Canadian nation by these United States by-product magazines. We have the very same Conservative opposition opposing this tax on advertising.
To go back in history for a minute, we will recall that when the Conservatives were last in power, from 1930 to 1935, one of the acts of the Conservative government of the day was to put a tax on all United States magazines coming into Canada. We will also recall that one of the first acts of the Liberal administration, when it came back into power in 1935, was to take off that tax. As the Prime Minister of that day very properly said, it is not in accordance with the principles of this government, this Liberal government, to put any tax on information coming into Canada. However, I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that anyone who faces the plain threat of these United States by-product publications, which are published half in Canada and half in the United States, can come to no other conclusion than that some such measures as are now proposed by the Minister of Finance are quite in order.
I would simply point out that if we take the 12 leading publications in Canada, including the all-United States by-product publications Time and Reader's Digest, at the beginning of the last seven-year period the United States publications between them had 20 per cent of the total advertising of that group. At the end of that seven-year period those same all-United States publications had 37 per cent of the total advertising in the whole of that group of leading magazines.
So I submit this. Of course, if we do not care whether or not we have in Canada vital, prosperous and thriving magazines; if we are simply willing to let the almighty dollar reach out on a catch as catch can basis, then we do not need to do anything about the menace to our own Canadian magazines. But believe me, the menace is very real indeed. For a country that is spending $30 million this year to keep the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in operation for the benefit of the Canadian people-and I venture to say there is not a single hon. member in this-

chamber who will not admit that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a great and necessary asset for this young Canadian nation-it is also in line to make sure that our Canadian magazines are allowed to survive, also in the national interest.
I have been a writer and journalist for more years than I sometimes care to remember, 33 years to be precise. I started with the Maclean Publishing Company. At one time in my life I worked for four years in Montreal for a very fine publication which I venture to say a good many members in this chamber have read. I refer to World Wide, just as good a magazine as Reader's Digest can ever hope to be. You will not find World Wide in publication now because it has been out of business for a good many years. I am happy to say that occurred after I left it. No publication with which I have been associated has ever failed while I have been with it, though some think they had a narrow escape.
You will not find World Wide in existence now, Mr. Speaker, but in that same city you will find Reader's Digest published. If you read the Canadian edition of Reader's Digest you will notice the strangest thing. You will notice that in the Canadian edition, which is almost but not quite identical with the United States edition, there is voluminous Canadian advertising. But if you read the United States edition of Reader's Digest you will not find any such advertising. Of course to anyone who studies the background facts the reason is quite simple. These United States publications which publish editions in Canada publish what are first, last and all the time by-products of their main American works. They are able to publish at a fraction of what you might call the fair cost of competition in this country. It is almost like using the tailings from a mine to fill out the main product.

speechtext:
I will be glad to answer questions at the end of my remarks, if my hon. friend wants to ask any. I venture to say that in no other line of business would we have tolerated for so long this strange form of competition against which our leading Canadian magazines are asked to compete. We heard today from the hon. member for York-Humber that the Minister of Finance perhaps had a tiger by the tail in having proposed a 20 per cent excise tax on these Canadian editions of United States magazines. I would say it was a truer description to say that these special Canadian editions of United States magazines almost constitute a tiger threatening our whole
The Budget-Mr. Philpott Canadian magazine field, and that we have to do something about the matter while we still have time.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I was certainly astonished by the remarks of that hard-headed publisher, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Nickle), who so often takes such an intelligent and sensible line in the house. On many occasions I think he takes a more sensible line than do his colleagues who sit around him, but naturally that is a matter of opinion. I wish to deal with his remarks about the tax on these special Canadian editions. I sometimes cah them fig leaf editions because the little maple leaf on their front cover hides their true identity to about the same extent that the fig leaf did on Eve.
I am bound to say that in my opinion the hon. member for Calgary South did not come up with a very practical suggestion. He suggested that instead of imposing a tax on these special Canadian editions of United States magazines we should set up a fund of $100,000 or $200,000, a government fund if you please, and that out of that government fund writers of merit who wrote for our Canadian magazines should receive certain grants. I can imagine the unholy howl that would have gone up from the opposition benches if that same suggestion had been made in the budget of the Minister of Finance. They would have said it was debauching the press, prostituting the press, trying to hire a stable of writers in favour of the government.
Let us be absolutely clear on the matter, Mi. Speaker. I have been a professional writer for a third of a century, and I for one am absolutely opposed to anything in the way of a subsidy fund to subsidize writers. I think we are going about the problem in a much more straightforward way by putting a straight excise tax of 20 per cent on these Canadian editions.
I agree with some of the points raised by the hon. member for Calgary South. It is quite true that some of our Canadian magazines could compete better if they were better run. I will not mention any names in that regard, but if I recall correctly Liberty magazine was first established here as the Canadian edition of the main United States job. However, when the parent publication folded up Liberty carried on as a purely Canadian publication, and it is doing a far better job as a purely all-Canadian proposition than it ever did as a by-product of the publication published in the United States. When I see fine magazines like Maclean's that are well able to hold their own as long as they have a fair field and no favours, then

The Budget-Mr. Philpott I think this 20 per cent tax goes at least part of the way toward restoring a fair field and no favours.
There was one suggestion made by the hon. member for York-Humber that I think is well worthy of at least further study. She pointed out that 91 United States publications come into Canada under the treaty whereby each country gives the other country free postal rights. As we all know, these things are governed by an international treaty to which nearly all nations subscribe. But when you recall that practically no Canadian magazine is able to ship its product in any numbers into the United States; when you recall that nearly 100 legitimate magazines, as I would call them, come into Canada from the United States and are afforded free postal rights under the general postal arrangements treaty, then I think it is time we took a good, long, second look at that treaty. In my opinion a good many of these magazines are certainly not sufficiently worth while to entitle them to a postal subsidy by the Dominion of Canada.
I for one would have been glad if the Minister of Finance in his 1956 budget had been able to bring in some of these whopping tax cuts which his predecessors made, or more of the very courageous cuts which he himself made last year, but when I had time to think the matter over I came to the conclusion that he was absolutely right-

Mr. Speaker, I want to say just a few words in English. All my notes are written in French. Of course, after I have spoken a few sentences you will realize that I am much more at ease when speaking my own language than when speaking the English language.
In my remarks on the budget I am not going to discuss it from its strictly financial aspect. That has been done in a masterly way by the Minister of Finance. We have heard spokesmen of the various parties sitting on the opposite side of this house. I wish to pay a certain tribute to the hon. member for Greenwood for the speech he delivered in this house. I do so not by reason of what he has said or by reason of any criticism he has made. He had a very bad cause to defend. He did it in a way that really took courage and at the same time a kind of spirit of invention to find some words with which to express a rather creditable criticism of such a good budget. I really congratulate him for having accomplished his task, though I am not going to admit that what he has said is really a true picture of the situation or that his suggestions represent the way this country should be administered financially.
Now, I also paid great attention to the hon. member for Lethbridge, who again explained the doctrine of social credit. Of course, according to his declaration, if we were to have the Social Credit party administer this country we would certainly be living in a kind of paradise, which I do not believe will ever exist under the sun. Sometimes strange coincidences do occur. On the same date that the present member for Lethbridge was delivering his speech, 20 years ago Mr. Aber-hart was declaring to Albertans that he could not give the dividend he had promised the citizens of that province. Really, I cannot see why the premier was not able to put into effect the policies which had won him the confidence of the citizens of his province.

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis Perhaps times were too hard, or perhaps conditions did not permit Mr. Aberhart to go ahead and distribute those dividends to the citizens of Alberta.
But now the hon. member for Lethbridge, to whom I always listen with great attention, has friends in the Alberta government. Perhaps with all these extra revenues the provincial government gets as a result of the discovery of oil it would be in a position to pay some dividends to the citizens of that province. I would suggest to the hon. member for Lethbridge that the present social credit government try, at least, to put into effect a promise which was made to Albertans 20 years ago and start to distribute dividends to the residents of that province.
I know it is the duty of the opposition to criticize the policies of the government. It is a right which-I do not know how it sounds in English but in French it goes very well- is sacred. In a democracy it is the privilege of the opposition to explain its point of view on any problems. However, I feel that once in a while we could expect from the opposite side of this chamber a fair dose of justice and logic; justice, by the recognition of subsequent actions of this government, and logic by trying to suggest measures that would certainly be of great advantage to this country. We should expect logic in this way, too, that the opposition would cease suggesting the lowering of taxes while at the same time asking this government to increase expenditures, especially in the field of health and welfare. Everybody from the opposite side of the house is asking for increased expenditures by every department of government, and at the same time expecting the government to decrease taxes. This is what I call illogical. I tried to find another word which would not be taken as an insult by those who do not believe as I do, but I could not find a softer word under the circumstances than "illogical".
Before each new budget is introduced we hear the people in all parts of this country asking, is the federal government going to lower taxes? Every year it is the same. I do not recall hearing one citizen in any province ask, is the provincial government going to lower taxes? Everybody has his eye on the federal field. Everybody wants the federal government to lower taxes. I want that too, and when the occasion comes I am glad to get a reduction in taxes.

Everybody is asking the federal government to decrease taxes. Every member on the opposite side of the house, and some members on this side, for instance, are also asking for an increase in family allowances. This is a very good thing, and I am in favour of it. maintopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE OF SUPPLY OF GARRY 27
speechtext: 1 am coming to that. I will answer the hon. member right away. Does the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre not know that the taxes collected by the federal government are turned back to the provinces in the proportion of 98 per cent? 1 would say that only a small percentage is kept for use outside of this country. Indirectly and directly all the taxes collected by the federal government are spent in the different provinces through public works, through different services and through tax agreements. According to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre it is only the C.C.F. party that is perfect. I do not think perfection exists in this world. All the provinces came to an agreement which was at least much more satisfactory than the one of a few years ago.
Mind you, it was only under this government, under the Liberal party, that this conference was brought about. Never before was there a question of distributing funds to the 67509-1721

speechtext: I will tell you one thing. I am not forgetting the British North America Act, and I wish my friends on the opposite side would remember that when they are discussing this question. They have come to the better understanding which exists today, although it is not perfect, although the provinces may not be entirely satisfied with the present situation. They wanted to administer their finances in the way that would be in the best interests of this country. It was on that basis that the agreements came into being. Maybe some 25, 30 or 40 years ago agreements could have been negotiated, but this time a solution was found. All the solutions to the big national problems have been found by this government, by the Liberal party. The C.C.F. party and the Social Credit party have made promises. We have found that they were promises which could never be realized. They could not be put into force during this prosperous time.

Answer by: Mr. Campney:
1.	Two types of commissions are granted in the regular force, namely short service commissions and permanent commissions. The type of commission granted depends upon education, the list or branch to which the candidate is appointed and, qualifications and requirements permitting, upon the wishes of the individual.
(a)	As a rule, short service commissions are granted initially to the following groups;
(i)	Aircrew who are not university or
Canadian services colleges graduates;
(ii)	Non-university graduate direct entrants of the flying control, ground observer, ground defence, and fighter controller branches;
(iii)	Female personnel, e.g., nurses and messing officers; and
(iv)	Doctors that do not want a permanent commission.
(b)	Normally, permanent commissions are granted to:
(i)	University or Canadian services colleges graduates entering any list or branch;
(ii)	Personnel promoted from the ranks, except those selected for aircrew training; and
(iii)	Officers holding short service commissions selected in competition towards the end of their engagement period.
Permanent commission boards are assembled semi-annually to review records of each short service commission officer who is within a year to a year and a half of termination of his period of service. Officers are then placed in three categories:
(a)	Suitable for permanent commissioning;
(b)	Suitable for a one-year extension; to be considered again for a permanent commission;
